danish.title: Trettende bog (1812) — Kapitel 7
paragraphs: Imens skulle en anden kolonne have angrebet franskmændene forfra, men Kutuzov ledsagede den kolonne. Han vidste udmærket, at der kun ville komme forvirring ud af dette slag, der var påbegyndt mod hans vilje, og i det omfang, det stod i hans magt, holdt han tropperne tilbage. Han rykkede ikke frem.
Han red tavst på sin lille grå hest og svarede dovent på forslag om at angribe.
»Ordet angreb ligger Dem altid på tungen, men De kan ikke se, at vi ikke er i stand til at udføre komplicerede manøvrer,« sagde han til Miloradovitj, der bad om tilladelse til at rykke frem.
»Vi kunne ikke tage Murat til fange i morges eller nå frem i tide, og nu kan der ikke gøres noget!« svarede han en anden.

Da Kutuzov blev informeret om, at der ved den franske bagtrop — hvor der ifølge kosakkernes rapporter tidligere ikke havde været nogen — nu stod to bataljoner polakker, kastede han et sideblik på Jermolov, der stod bag ham, og som han ikke havde talt med siden dagen før.
»Ser De! De beder om at angribe og lægger alle mulige planer, men så snart man kommer i gang, er intet klar, og fjenden, advaret i forvejen, tager sine forholdsregler.«
Jermolov kneb øjnene sammen og smilede svagt ved disse ord. Han forstod, at stormen var blæst over for hans vedkommende, og at Kutuzov ville nøjes med den antydning.
»Han morer sig lidt på min bekostning,« sagde Jermolov stille og puffede med sit knæ til Rajevskij, der stod ved hans side.
Kort efter gik Jermolov hen til Kutuzov og bemærkede ærbødigt:
»Det er endnu ikke for sent, Deres Durchlauchtighed — fjenden er ikke draget bort — hvis De ville beordre et angreb! Ellers får garden ikke så meget som et glimt af røg.«
Kutuzov svarede ikke, men da man rapporterede til ham, at Murats tropper var i tilbagetog, beordrede han en fremrykning, skønt han ved hver hundrede skridt holdt inde i tre kvarter.
Hele slaget bestod i, hvad Orlov-Denisovs kosakker havde udrettet: resten af hæren mistede blot nogle hundrede mand til ingen nytte.

Som følge af dette slag modtog Kutuzov en diamantdekoration, og Bennigsen nogle diamanter og hundrede tusind rubler; andre modtog ligeledes behagelige anerkendelser svarende til deres respektive grader, og efter slaget blev der foretaget nye ændringer i staben.

»Sådan gør man alting hos os, alt på hovedet!« sagde de russiske officerer og generaler efter slaget ved Tarutino, idet de lod forstå, at en eller anden tåbe deroppe gør alting forkert, mens vi selv ikke ville have gjort sådan, ganske som folk taler i dag. Men folk, der taler sådan, ved enten ikke, hvad de taler om, eller bedrager bevidst sig selv. Intet slag — Tarutino, Borodinó eller Austerlitz — forløber, som de, der planlagde det, havde forudset. Det er en grundbetingelse.

Et utal af frie kræfter (for ingensteds er mennesket friere end under et slag, hvor det drejer sig om liv og død) påvirker kampens forløb, og det forløb kan aldrig kendes på forhånd og falder aldrig sammen med retningen af en enkelt kraft.

Når mange samtidige og forskelligt rettede kræfter virker på et givet legeme, kan dets bevægelsesretning ikke falde sammen med nogen enkelt af disse kræfter, men vil altid være en middel — hvad der i mekanikken fremstilles som diagonalen i et kraftparallellogram.

Når vi i historikernes beskrivelser, især de franske, finder, at deres krige og slag blev gennemført i overensstemmelse med på forhånd lagte planer, er den eneste slutning, der kan drages, at disse beskrivelser er falske.

Slaget ved Tarutino opnåede åbenbart ikke det mål, Toll havde haft for øje — at føre tropperne i kamp i den rækkefølge, dispositionerne foreskrev; heller ikke det, grev Orlov-Denisov måtte have haft — at tage Murat til fange; heller ikke det øjeblikkelige resultat at tilintetgøre hele korpset, som Bennigsen og andre måtte have haft for øje; heller ikke den officers mål, der ønskede at gå i kamp for at udmærke sig; heller ikke kosakkens, der ville have mere bytte, end han fik; og så videre. Men hvis slagets mål var det, der faktisk blev resultatet, og som alle russere den dag ønskede — at drive franskmændene ud af Rusland og tilintetgøre deres hær — er det ganske klart, at slaget ved Tarutino, netop på grund af dets uoverensstemmelser, var præcis det, der trængtes til på det tidspunkt af felttoget. Det ville være vanskeligt og endda umuligt at forestille sig et mere gunstigt resultat end det faktiske udfald af dette slag. Med et minimum af indsats og ubetydelige tab, og trods den største forvirring, blev felttogets vigtigste resultater opnået: overgangen fra tilbagetog til fremrykning, en afsløring af franskmændenes svaghed og indgivelsen af det stød, som Napoleons hær kun havde ventet på for at begynde sin flugt.

english.title: Book Thirteen (1812) — Chapter 7
paragraphs: Meanwhile, another column was supposed to attack the French from the front, but Kutuzov accompanied it. He knew perfectly well that nothing but chaos would come of this battle fought against his will, and as far as he could, he held the troops back. He did not advance.
He rode silently on his small gray horse, lazily brushing off suggestions that they should attack.
'You always want to attack, but you don't see that we're incapable of carrying out complicated maneuvers,' he said to Miloradovich, who asked permission to advance.
'We couldn't capture Murat this morning or get to our positions in time, and nothing can be done now!' he told someone else.

When Kutuzov was informed that behind the French rear—where, according to the Cossacks' reports, there had been nobody before—two Polish battalions had now appeared, he shot a sidelong glance at Ermolov, who was behind him and to whom he hadn't spoken since the day before.
'You see! They keep asking to attack and making all kinds of plans, but as soon as it comes to action, nothing is ready, and the enemy, forewarned, takes countermeasures.'
Ermolov narrowed his eyes and smiled faintly at these words. He understood that the storm had passed for him, and that Kutuzov would be satisfied with just this hint.
'He's having a little fun at my expense,' Ermolov said quietly, nudging Raevsky with his knee.
Shortly after, Ermolov approached Kutuzov and remarked respectfully:
'It's not too late yet, Your Highness—the enemy hasn't pulled back. If you would order an attack! Otherwise the Guards won't even get a glimpse of smoke.'
Kutuzov didn't respond, but when they reported that Murat's troops were retreating, he ordered an advance—though he halted for three-quarters of an hour at every hundred paces.
The entire battle amounted to what Orlov-Denisov's Cossacks had accomplished. The rest of the army simply lost a few hundred men for nothing.

As a result of this battle, Kutuzov received a diamond decoration, Bennigsen received diamonds and a hundred thousand rubles, and others received pleasant rewards according to their rank. After the battle, fresh staff changes were made.

'That's how everything is done with us—all upside down!' said the Russian officers and generals after the Battle of Tarutino, suggesting that some fool had done things all wrong but that they themselves would never have blundered so—just as people talk today. But those who say such things either don't know what they're talking about or are deliberately fooling themselves. No battle—Tarutino, Borodino, or Austerlitz—ever goes as its planners expected. That is a fundamental truth.

A countless number of free forces (for nowhere is a man freer than in battle, where life and death hang in the balance) shape the course of a fight, and that course can never be known in advance and never coincides with any single force's direction.

If many forces act simultaneously on a body from different directions, the resulting movement cannot coincide with any one of them but will always be an average—what mechanics represents as the diagonal of a parallelogram of forces.
If we find in historians' accounts—especially French ones—that their wars and battles went according to prearranged plans, the only conclusion we can draw is that those accounts are false.

The Battle of Tarutino clearly didn't achieve Toll's aim of leading the troops into action according to the dispositions; nor Count Orlov-Denisov's possible aim of capturing Murat; nor Bennigsen's goal of immediately destroying the entire corps; nor the ambitions of the officer eager to distinguish himself; nor the Cossack's wish for more loot. But if the aim of the battle was what actually resulted and what all Russians desired—to drive the French out of Russia and destroy their army—then it's quite clear that the Battle of Tarutino, precisely because of its confusion, was exactly what was needed at that stage of the campaign. It would be difficult, even impossible, to imagine a better outcome. With minimal effort and insignificant losses, despite the greatest disorder, the most important results of the entire campaign were achieved: the transition from retreat to advance, the exposure of French weakness, and the delivery of that shock Napoleon's army had been waiting for to begin its flight.
